props.title: 13 Lakes
props.initialSlug: 13 stunning American lakes filmed in pristine silence

sections.content: James Benning's 13 Lakes (2004) revolutionized structural filmmaking through radical simplicity. Each of its 13 ten-minute static shots frames a different American lake, challenging viewers' perception of time and landscape. This approach builds on Andy Warhol's Empire (1964), which filmed the Empire State Building for 8 hours, but Benning adds natural dynamism - shifting light, rippling water, passing clouds. The film connects to other landmark landscape works like Peter Hutton's Time and Tide (2000) and Sharon Lockhart's Double Tide (2009), showing how patient observation reveals hidden rhythms in seemingly static scenes.

sections.content: Benning's approach influenced a new wave of slow cinema. Directors like Lav Diaz with Evolution of a Filipino Family (2004) and Tsai Ming-liang's Stray Dogs (2013) embraced extended duration and minimal action. 13 Lakes stripped cinema to its essence - light, time, and space. Each lake becomes a living canvas, revealing how subtle environmental changes create natural drama. The film demands and rewards patience, training viewers to notice minute details that commercial cinema typically ignores.

The environmental implications of 13 Lakes resonate strongly with contemporary eco-cinema. Films like Jennifer Baichwal's Watermark (2013) and Viktor Kossakovsky's Aquarela (2018) build on Benning's contemplative approach to landscape, though with more conventional structures. Benning's pure observational method captures America's diverse waterways without commentary, letting viewers confront their own relationship with natural spaces. SUBHEAD: Impact on Contemporary Experimental Cinema

13 Lakes helped establish a new vocabulary for experimental landscape films. Works like James Benning's own small roads (2011) and Peter Hutton's At Sea (2007) demonstrate how patient observation can reveal profound truths about place and perception. The film's influence extends beyond experimental circles - Gus Van Sant's "Death Trilogy" (Gerry (2002), Elephant (2003), Last Days (2005)) employs similar techniques of extended duration and environmental immersion.
